clue.text: High positions for Sun-follower politicians

blocks.note: pro means in favour of
Monday follows Sunday; MON is its short form
Tories are members of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: Politicians who follow the Sun newspaper line are rewarded with lofty posts.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun looks like the tabloid newspaper, but its follower is the day after Sunday. Tories are Britain's Conservative politicians.
explanation.definitionFit: Headlands jutting out from a coast are raised points of land, so they are lofty spots in a landscape.

clue.text: Helping to keep old books moving around

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold it inside, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a helping or portion of food
OT is the Old Testament, the old books of the Bible

explanation.surface: Someone lends a hand keeping a stock of old books in circulation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Helping' reads as a verb but is the noun for a portion. OT for Old Testament is a crossword standard.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotation is turning in a circle or taking turns in sequence, which is a noun sense of going round.

clue.text: What gives fellow energy? Certainly in the case of Samson!

definitions.text: What gives fellow energy? Certainly in the case of Samson!

blocks.note: a fellow is a man
E is the symbol for energy in physics

explanation.surface: A riddle about what makes a man strong, with Samson as the example.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: the fellow plus energy builds the word, and Samson's strength famously lay in his long uncut hair.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Bible story Samson lost his strength when his long locks were shorn, so his head of hair gave him power.

clue.text: A port that could be Salerno

definitions.text: A port that could be Salerno

blocks.clueFragment: A port that could be Salerno
blocks.note: surface reading: a harbour town that might be the Italian port of Salerno
setter's reading: rearrange the letters of Salerno and the result is a fresh version of a French city's name, which names an American port

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a particular port might turn out to be Salerno in Italy.
explanation.walkthrough: Salerno is a real Italian port, which sends you to Italy; instead its letters remade give Orleans, and a remade Orleans is a new one.
explanation.definitionFit: The Louisiana city on the Mississippi is a major American river port, handling huge amounts of shipping cargo.

clue.text: Things heard in church making gran so screwed up

indicators.note: something screwed up is crumpled and disordered, so the letters lose their order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Noises in church that leave grandmother so flustered and upset.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Screwed up' seems to describe the flustered gran, but it tells you to rearrange her letters with the word after.
explanation.definitionFit: Pipe instruments played during services are the classic musical sound of a church building.

clue.text: I complete story about Saint to be used in worship

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps round another

blocks.note: taken as written
to do a task is to complete it
a lie is a made-up story
S is the abbreviation for saint

explanation.surface: Someone finishing a tale about a saint that will be read during a service.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a church reading; 'worship' at the end is a verb, not a service.
explanation.definitionFit: To idolise someone is to adore them excessively, treating them like a god, which is to worship them.

clue.text: What will give you wonderful lawns? These folk will offer information

definitions.text: What will give you wonderful lawns?

blocks.clueFragment: What will give you wonderful lawns?
blocks.note: first meaning: excellent turf, read literally as two words
second meaning: criminals who inform on many associates to the police

explanation.walkthrough: The first half is a whimsical literal split of the word into super and grasses; a supergrass is British slang for an informer who betrays many criminals at once.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a grass is a police informer, and a supergrass informs on a whole gang, often for immunity.

clue.text: Bit of food that has fish served up after gym

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from bottom to top, backwards

blocks.note: PE is physical education, school gym
a tuna is a fish

explanation.surface: A snack with fish on it, eaten after a gym session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Served up' sounds like dishing out food, but in a down clue it turns the fish upside down. The order is gym first, since the fish comes after it.
explanation.definitionFit: A single groundnut is a small snack item, so it is a morsel one might eat.

clue.text: Attend, being exhausted

blocks.note: first meaning, read as two words: to be present at something
second meaning: informally, worn out

explanation.walkthrough: The first meaning only works if the answer is split into two small words, be and at, which together mean to attend.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally, being beat means being tired out, a colloquial sense common in Britain and America.

clue.text: Bloggers en masse? Only half seem grown up, sadly

indicators.note: keeping only half of a word means dropping the rest of its letters
sadly suggests things have gone wrong, so the letters end up in a bad order

blocks.note: the first half of the word, its first two letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: A lament that only half of all bloggers seem to be mature adults.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Only half' looks like it refers to the bloggers, but it trims the next word. The question mark flags a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: An online discussion forum where many users post messages is a crowd of internet writers gathered together.

clue.text: I can’t hit a pet — somehow that would be hostile

indicators.note: somehow means in some unspecified way, so the letters come out in an unknown order

blocks.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe and spaces

explanation.surface: A pet owner refusing to strike an animal because it would be cruel.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe and spaces in the first four words are ignored; all twelve letters are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Antipathy is strong dislike, so feeling it toward someone means being opposed and unfriendly to them.

clue.text: Pieces of music being performed in practice sessions

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another

blocks.note: a show that is on is being performed
in cricket, nets are practice sessions in netted enclosures

explanation.surface: Musical pieces played during rehearsals.
explanation.walkthrough: Nets is a cricket term: batting practice takes place in netted lanes, so the sessions themselves are called nets.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonet is a composition written for nine instruments or voices, so it is a musical work.

clue.text: Finish in German city that’s more fashionable

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another

blocks.note: the end is the finish
Trier is an old city in western Germany

explanation.surface: Ending up in a German city that is more stylish than others.
explanation.walkthrough: Trier, on the Moselle, is one of Germany's oldest cities and a handy crossword source.
explanation.definitionFit: Trendy means following the latest style, and the comparative form means more in vogue.

clue.text: ‘Kill, burn!’, he explodes in battle

indicators.note: an explosion scatters its material, so the letters fly apart and land rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A soldier shouting kill and burn as he goes berserk in the fighting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Explodes' fits the battlefield picture but is the anagram signal; the punctuation around the shouted words is ignored.
explanation.definitionFit: The 1775 engagement near Boston was an early major clash of the American Revolutionary War.

clue.text: Launches fantastic reductions

indicators.note: fantastic means fanciful or bizarre, so the letters take a strange new form

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A shop advertising the start of a sale with amazing price cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fantastic reductions' reads as a sale slogan, but the adjective is the anagram signal for the noun.
explanation.definitionFit: To bring a new product or scheme into use for the first time is to start it off.

clue.text: It’s better avoided by one who doesn’t want alcohol

definitions.text: It’s better avoided by one who doesn’t want alcohol

indicators.text: avoided by one who doesn’t want alcohol
indicators.note: a teetotaller is called TT, so what such a person steers clear of is a pair of Ts, which are removed

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sensible warning that a drink is best steered clear of by a non-drinker.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition and the wordplay at once: TT is the standard shorthand for teetotal, so a teetotal version of the word drops both its Ts.
explanation.definitionFit: A pint of ale or lager is exactly the kind of alcoholic drink a non-drinker would refuse.

clue.text: I am at home getting stuck into bowl in sink

indicators.note: something stuck into another thing is lodged within it

blocks.note: contraction of I am
someone at home is in
a bowl is a dish

explanation.surface: Someone at home tucking into a bowl of food at the kitchen sink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sink' looks like the kitchen fitting beside the bowl, but it is a verb meaning to decline.
explanation.definitionFit: To decrease or grow less is to decline in value or amount, as prices or hopes can.

clue.text: Atmosphere by far side of the river

indicators.note: the far side of a word is its end, so only its final letter is taken

blocks.note: the atmosphere is the air
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: The atmosphere on the opposite bank of a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Aire is a river in Yorkshire in northern England, flowing through Leeds.
explanation.definitionFit: The Aire is a Yorkshire waterway that flows through Leeds before joining the Ouse.

clue.text: Soldier to pull up, having got back outside

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means reading from the bottom, so backwards
outside means surrounding, so one piece wraps around the other

blocks.note: the back is the rear
to lug is to pull or drag

explanation.surface: A soldier told to haul himself upright after getting back to base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pull up' reads as halt, but 'up' turns the pulling word over, and 'back' is a noun, not 'return'.
explanation.definitionFit: A regular is a member of a standing professional army, as opposed to a reservist or volunteer.

clue.text: Underwater explorers sink at sea — several

indicators.note: being at sea means confused and lost, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written
divers is an old word meaning several or sundry

explanation.surface: Several divers going down in the ocean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At sea' sits naturally with underwater explorers but is the anagram signal. Divers here is the old adjective for various, not people diving.
explanation.definitionFit: Skin-divers swim below the surface without a diving suit, often with just mask and fins, exploring the depths.

clue.text: Little bird to nibble, full of endless joy

indicators.note: without an end, so the final letter is dropped
something full of another thing holds it inside

blocks.note: to nibble is to eat
glee means joy; here its last letter is lost

explanation.surface: A small bird pecking at food, overflowing with happiness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little bird' is not a tit or wren: it is a young bird of a big species.
explanation.definitionFit: An eaglet is a young eagle, so it is a small, immature bird of prey.

clue.text: Fiery sailor needs to take it easy

blocks.note: AB is an able seaman, an able-bodied sailor
to laze is to relax idly

explanation.surface: A hot-tempered sailor is told he must calm down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiery' suggests a temperament, but the answer means literally on fire. AB for a sailor is a crossword standard.
explanation.definitionFit: Something ablaze is burning brightly, in flames, so it is on fire or glowing with heat.

clue.text: Like many a noble type‘s greeting, conveyed audibly

indicators.note: audibly means as heard, so the words count by their sound

blocks.note: hi is a greeting
something conveyed is carried, or borne

explanation.surface: An aristocrat's hello, delivered out loud.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are sound-alikes: the greeting and the past participle of carry.
explanation.definitionFit: Nobles typically inherit their rank from aristocratic parents, so most are of lofty birth and lineage.

clue.text: Celebrate having left spouse finally, becoming this?

definitions.text: Celebrate having left spouse finally, becoming this?

indicators.note: finally points to the last position, so only the closing letter is taken

blocks.note: to celebrate in song
L is the abbreviation for left
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone celebrating after walking out on their husband or wife, now unattached.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: the state you reach after leaving a spouse. 'Left' reads as departed but gives L.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has walked out of a marriage is unattached and no longer part of a couple.

clue.text: Report of prominent Lib Dem being cut down

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the word counts by its sound

blocks.note: Chris Huhne was a leading Liberal Democrat politician and cabinet minister

explanation.surface: News that a leading Liberal Democrat has been brought low.
explanation.walkthrough: Chris Huhne was a prominent Liberal Democrat, a British centrist party, and served as Energy Secretary; 'cut down' also hints at his political fall.
explanation.definitionFit: Hewn is the past participle of hew, meaning chopped with an axe, as trees are felled.

clue.text: Work’s ending at four — with story going round that’s gossipy

indicators.note: the ending of a word is its final letter
going round something means surrounding it, so one piece encloses others

blocks.note: a tale is a story
the final letter of the word
taken as written
IV is four in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Office chatter as the working day ends at four, with a rumour doing the rounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work's ending at four' reads as knocking-off time, but it gives a letter, a word and a Roman numeral.
explanation.definitionFit: A person fond of chatting and passing on rumours is chatty, inclined to talk a great deal.

clue.text: I lose hope with couple leaving — a fateful day!

indicators.note: something leaving goes away, so those letters are taken out

blocks.note: I despair means I lose hope
a couple is a pair

explanation.surface: Someone in despair as a couple walks out, on a doom-laden day.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ides of March was the day Julius Caesar was assassinated, after the soothsayer's warning to beware it.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Roman calendar the Ides fell mid-month; Caesar's murder on that date made it proverbially ominous.

clue.text: Central beach could offer total freedom

indicators.note: what something could offer is a possible alternative form, so the letters may be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A beach in the middle of town might give visitors a sense of liberty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Could offer' looks like a link between wordplay and definition, but it signals that the two words may be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase literally means a blank paper, signed so the holder can write any terms, hence unlimited authority.
